boundary_rationale: Opens with the refrain at 19:1, correctly placed at a chapter line ahead of a new, previously unseen protagonist, but the refrain's own construction is now stated accurately rather than assimilated to 18:1's. 19:1 reads וַיְהִי֙ בַּיָּמִ֣ים הָהֵ֔ם וּמֶ֖לֶךְ אֵ֣ין בְּיִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל - a wayehi-prefixed clause with the constituents inverted (וּמֶלֶךְ אֵין rather than אֵין מֶלֶךְ), continuing after the athnach into a second, parallel וַיְהִי clause (וַיְהִ֣י אִ֣ישׁ לֵוִ֗י גָּ֚ר) rather than fusing with the new subject in one sentence. This is a third distinct realization of the short-form refrain, differing from both 18:1 (which achieves its cohesion by repeating the bare temporal adverbial, בַּיָּמִ֣ים הָהֵ֔ם / וּבַיָּמִ֣ים הָהֵ֗ם, with no wayehi and no inversion) and from the plain form at 17:6/21:25. The binding argument therefore differs verse by verse and must be stated for each: 18:1 binds by adverbial repetition, 19:1 binds by a parallel wayehi construction with inverted word order. Narrates the concubine's infidelity and departure, and the Levite's pursuit. Closes with the father's joyful welcome (v3), whose closing verb (וְלֹֽא)-object (לְהָשִׁיבָ֔הּ 'to bring her back') follows the qere against a ketiv reading להשיבו, now disclosed rather than silently adopted. v4 opens the father-in-law's extended hospitality, a new phase - a mild reset (participant respecified with a new kinship term one verse after his first appearance) rather than a strong formulaic marker.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Unchanged in conclusion: treating the refrain clause as its own micro-decision, mirroring 18:1, was considered and rejected - but not, as previously stated, 'for the identical reason given there,' since 18:1 and 19:1 are not built the same way. The refrain principle is restated in functional terms: the two-clause full form (17:6, 21:25) comments and closes; the one-clause short form heads a new complex, realized differently at its two outings (adverbial repetition at 18:1, an inverted-order wayehi clause at 19:1).

boundary_rationale: Opens with the abrupt violent intrusion (v22), a scene deliberately echoing Genesis 19's Sodom narrative, and narrates the host's offer of the women instead, the mob's refusal to listen, and the assault. v25's grammatical subject is corrected a second time here: הָאִישׁ ('the man') is not disambiguated by the noun alone - the same designation is used for the guest (the Levite) at 19:7 and 19:9 and for the householder at 19:22-19:23, so 'the man' who seizes and puts out the concubine in v25 could, on the bare noun, be either. The possessive suffix on the object phrase, בְּפִילַגְשׁוֹ ('his concubine'), favors the Levite as the intended referent, since she is identified as his concubine throughout and the pronoun most naturally binds to the clause's own subject; but this is a lean, not a settled identification, and the row no longer states flatly that the host is 'the grammatical subject of both verbs.' What is secure regardless of which man performs the act is that she is the object throughout, not the agent of her own surrender. Closes with her collapse at the threshold 'until it was light' (v26), the atrocity's aftermath visible before the Levite wakes. v27 opens his discovery the next morning. Neither edge of this span carries admissible external evidence: WEB runs 19:21 together with 19:22 and 19:26 together with 19:27, opening paragraphs instead at 19:23 and 19:25 - disclosed as non-driving metadata under m8-mesh-r2, and in any case interior to the span rather than at either of its own edges - and this chapter carries no parashah mark before the petuchah after 19:30. With the internal escalating-scene argument as the only ground actually carrying the span, and no admissible witness at either edge, confidence is repriced from high to medium.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Unchanged: splitting the demand-and-negotiation (22-24) from the assault itself (25-26) was considered and rejected; both halves form one uninterrupted escalating scene of violence with no participant or location change.

strongest_rejected_alternative: The Levite's testimony and the assembly's resolution in 8-11 might read as one accusation-and-response span; that doesn't survive v8's turn to 'All the people arose as one man,' a clear speaker-change from individual witness to collective assembly that keeps testimony apart from the deliberation it provokes.

strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding the ultimatum to Benjamin (12-13) into this resolution unit as its direct continuation was considered; rejected because v12's messengers sent to Benjamin is a distinct diplomatic overture addressed to a specific party, not a further elaboration of the assembly's internal oath-taking.

strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching this exchange to the assembly's resolution (157) as one continuous planning span was considered; rejected because the ultimatum is addressed to a specific named party with its own distinct request-and-refusal structure, a self-contained diplomatic beat.

boundary_rationale: A single-verse inquiry scene at Bethel: 'Who shall go up for us first to battle against the children of Benjamin?' This decision discloses a deliberate resumptive echo of the book's opening inquiry formula at 1:1-2, now stated precisely rather than overstated. The verbatim recurrence lives in the question-formula (מִ֚י יַעֲלֶה לָּ֣נוּ...בַתְּחִלָּ֔ה, near-identical to 1:1's מִ֣י יַעֲלֶה לָּ֧נוּ...בַּתְּחִלָּ֖ה), not in the answer: 1:2 gives יְהוּדָ֣ה יַעֲלֶ֑ה plus an attached land-grant clause, while 20:18 gives the shorter יְהוּדָ֥ה בַתְּחִלָּֽה, migrating the adverb בַתְּחִלָּה from the question into the answer rather than repeating 1:2's verb יַעֲלֶה. The two answers share only the named tribe and the shared opener וַיֹּ֥אמֶר יְהוָ֖ה יְהוּדָ֣ה. The civil war against a fellow Israelite tribe is still framed by a deliberate reuse of the conquest-opening oracle formula - an ironic structural signal - but the frame is a resumptive echo of the question, not a verbatim doubling of the whole exchange. Opens on the shift from troop-counting to cultic inquiry; closes before v19's fresh muster-and-encampment notice.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Unchanged: merging this oracle into the troop-muster unit (159) as its natural sequel was considered and rejected; the oracle is a discrete cultic act formally distinct from the numerical muster-register just completed, and its near-verbatim echo of 1:1's question-formula merits isolation as its own decision.

oshb:Judg.1.1 מִ֣י יַעֲלֶה לָּ֧נוּ אֶל הַֽכְּנַעֲנִ֛י בַּתְּחִלָּ֖ה — cited for the verbatim question-formula echo

strongest_rejected_alternative: The first and second battle days, 19-21 and 22-25, could be told as one early-battles span; v22 opens its own encouragement-and-second-inquiry sequence marking a new day's preparation, consistent with how the war's three engagements are kept distinct elsewhere.

Closes with the third inquiry and Yahweh's promise of victory, 'Go up; for tomorrow I will deliver him into your hand' (v28)-the turning point after two devastating defeats. v29 shifts to the ambush strategy's actual implementation.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating the genealogical aside (v27b-28a) as a separate decision from the mourning-ritual and inquiry was considered; rejected because the aside is a parenthetical clause embedded within the single continuous sentence reporting the inquiry, not a self-standing unit.

Closes with that realization (v41), a suspense-building climax. v42 opens the rout and pursuit itself, a shift from realization to flight.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the ambush's assault on the city (35-38) from Benjamin's dawning realization (39-41) was considered; rejected because both halves are deliberately interwoven by the narrator, describing the ambushers' actions and Benjamin's simultaneous, unaware continued fighting, as one synchronized dramatic sequence building to the shared moment of recognition.

boundary_rationale: Opens with Benjamin's flight 'before the men of Israel to the way of the wilderness' (v42), a shift from realization to physical retreat, and narrates the relentless pursuit with successive, layered casualty figures. The clause opening v45 (וַיִּפְנ֞וּ וַיָּנֻ֤סוּ הַמִּדְבָּ֨רָה֙ אֶל סֶ֣לַע הָֽרִמּ֔וֹן) recurs byte-identical at v47 - Wiederaufnahme in its purest form in this range - with v46's summary casualty tally (אֶֽת כָּל אֵ֖לֶּה אַנְשֵׁי חָֽיִל, twenty-five thousand who drew the sword) sitting inside the bracket the repetition forms rather than at a genuine boundary. The unit now runs through the survivors' flight to the rock of Rimmon and the four-month refuge there (v47), and the war's final act of destruction, the remaining Benjaminite towns burned (v48). Closes at the petuchah after v48, confirmed present in both witnesses, where the war itself ends. Ch21:1 opens a new temporal-thematic register, beginning the resolution.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Unchanged in its own terms, now subsuming the alternative previously argued at 167: extending this unit through v48 was previously rejected on the ground that v46's tally is a complete rhetorical closure and v47 opens a distinguishable coda about the surviving remnant. That rejection is withdrawn: v47 is not a fresh narrowing-focus onset but the second half of the verbatim resumptive pair whose first half sits at v45, inside this unit, so no boundary can be drawn between them. The unit closes instead at v48, at the petuchah, where the war narrative itself ends and ch21's resolution begins.

boundary_rationale: Opens with the retrospective oath-notice, 'Now the men of Israel had sworn in Mizpah, saying, None of us will give his daughter to Benjamin as a wife'-a flashback clause establishing the legal problem the rest of the chapter must solve-then the assembly's grief at Bethel and their direct lament to Yahweh, 'why has this happened in Israel, that there should be one tribe lacking in Israel today?' Closes with that lament (v3). v4 opens a new ritual action, altar-building, shifting from speech to cultic response.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The altar-building unit of 4-7 could be read together with this one as a single mourning-and-cultic-response span; v4's 'On the next day, the people rose early and built an altar' marks a fresh temporal, action-based beat apart from the lament-speech of 1-3.

boundary_rationale: The seam is moved rather than the two decisions merged. This decision now covers only the cultic response: 'On the next day, the people rose early and built an altar there, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings' (וַֽיְהִי֙ מִֽמָּחֳרָ֔ת וַיַּשְׁכִּ֣ימוּ הָעָ֔ם וַיִּבְנוּ שָׁ֖ם מִזְבֵּ֑חַ), a self-contained ritual beat opened by an unambiguous next-day temporal marker and closed by the offerings themselves, corroborated by a petuchah confirmed present after Judg.21.4 in both witnesses. The practical crisis and its restated deliberation - previously folded into this span through v7 - move to M8-Judg-170, which now opens at v5 and carries its own legal warrant (the מוֹת יוּמָת penalty clause) inside its own boundary rather than borrowed from across a seam.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Two arrangements were weighed. (a) Merging 169 and 170 outright into one Judg.21.4-Judg.21.12 span was considered, since the altar-building and the enquiry that follows it are causally continuous. (b) Re-closing 169 at v4 alone and opening 170 at v5 was preferred instead: it resolves the internal inconsistency (170's own causal argument no longer depends on a clause quarantined in the neighboring decision) without collapsing two distinguishable beats - a discrete ritual act (altar and offerings) versus a discrete investigative-and-punitive sequence (the restated question through the raid's completion) - into one. The fixed record can carry the seam once it sits at v4/v5 instead of v7/v8, so the merge is not required.
boundary_evidence_refs: oshb:Judg.21.4 וַֽיְהִי֙ מִֽמָּחֳרָ֔ת וַיַּשְׁכִּ֣ימוּ הָעָ֔ם וַיִּבְנוּ שָׁ֖ם מִזְבֵּ֑חַ וַיַּעֲל֥וּ עֹל֖וֹת וּשְׁלָמִֽים
parashah_two_witness: pe after Judg.21.4 (weak corroboration, Prophets - aligns with this span's own close, now that the span ends at v4)

boundary_rationale: Opens with the investigative question restated in full, now including its own legal basis: וַיֹּֽאמְרוּ֙ בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל מִ֠י אֲשֶׁ֨ר לֹא עָלָ֧ה בַקָּהָ֛ל מִכָּל שִׁבְטֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל אֶל יְהוָ֑ה (v5), which carries the מוֹת יוּמָת death-penalty clause the raid on Jabesh Gilead depends on - previously cited as this decision's warrant while sitting, inconsistently, inside the neighboring span. The question is put again in near-identical wording at v8 (מִ֗י אֶחָד֙ מִשִּׁבְטֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אֲשֶׁ֛ר לֹֽא עָלָ֥ה אֶל יְהוָ֖ה הַמִּצְפָּ֑ה) once the specific absent tribe is identified - a lexical and thematic resumption of the question first posed at v5, restating rather than initiating the inquiry. The punitive expedition follows directly: twelve thousand men sent to destroy Jabesh Gilead except its unmarried women (the survivors are what the command at v11 leaves over, not an exception written into the order itself). Closes with the delivery of four hundred young women to the camp at Shiloh (v12), corroborated by a setumah confirmed present in both witnesses. v13 opens a new diplomatic act, the peace overture to Benjamin at Rimmon.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the census-discovery (5-9) from the raid's execution and result (10-12) was considered and rejected, as before; both halves form one uninterrupted cause-and-consequence sequence with no scene-break. The alternative newly resolved here is the opening edge itself: opening at v8 (as originally drafted) was tested and rejected, because v8 restates rather than initiates the question already posed at v5, and this decision's own reasoning about the Mizpah oath's penalty clause requires v5 to be read as part of the same unit that acts on it.

The close does not rest on a 'new speaker' at v19: 21:19 opens וַיֹּאמְר֡וּ with no expressed subject, continuing the elders introduced at v16 by inflection exactly as v17 does. literature_type_guess: dispersal notice and closing refrain (book-ending inclusio)
boundary_rationale: Opens with the general Israelite dispersal (v24), a wider closing notice bringing the civil-war-and-resolution narrative to a peaceful end - a genuine explicit-subject reset from the Benjaminite subject of 21:23 (בְּנֵי בִנְיָמִן) to the Israelite subject of 21:24 (בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל), the criterion this campaign treats as decisive at this unit's opening edge exactly as it does elsewhere (e.g. M8-Judg-001, M8-Judg-061). No external mark corroborates that edge - WEB's own paragraph break falls at 21:23, inside the preceding decision, and runs unbroken through 21:24-25, and this chapter's parashah marks (pe after 21:4; samekh after 21:12, 21:18, 21:22) fall short of it - but the reset itself is a text-internal signal, not metadata, and stands as this edge's driver on its own terms. Closes with the book's final verse, the full-form refrain repeated verbatim from 17:6 - confirmed byte-identical under NFC, cantillation included, so the inclusio claim here is exact rather than approximate - and that inclusio is this closing edge's own driver: unlike a successor-contrast signal, it does not require anything to follow, since it corroborates the unit's terminus by bracketing back to 17:6 rather than by distinguishing this unit from what comes next. That is the operative difference from M8-Judg-001's opening edge, whose own inclusio (with 20:18) likewise cannot resolve it, but for the opposite reason: 1:1 is the book's first verse, and a live boundary question stands open behind it (Joshua's narrative continues there), which no backward-looking bracket internal to Judges can settle. Nothing follows 21:25 at all, so no comparable live question remains open on this side; the closing question is fixed by the physical end of the text, and the inclusio is the affirmative signal that this ending is the deliberate, marked counterpart of 17:6 rather than an arbitrary stopping point. With a stated driver at each of its own two edges - the explicit-subject reset at 23/24 and the inclusio at the close - this decision's HIGH grade holds on text-internal grounds. This decision also notes the decision's structural echo of 20:18's frame with 1:1-2; that secondary reference now carries the correction made at M8-Judg-160: the 1:1-2/20:18 pairing is a deliberate resumptive echo concentrated in the question-formula (מִי יַעֲלֶה לָּנוּ...בַּתְּחִלָּה) and the shared opener, not a pair of verbally identical answers as previously overstated. The 17:6/21:25 pairing itself, and this decision's own span, confidence, and primary evidence, are untouched by that correction.
